Trends in the Health Workforce Supply in the Rural U.S. 1 Policy Report • October 2024 KEY FINDINGS Trends in the Supply of Rural Health Workforce Nationally, the supply per 100,000 population of primary care physicians (including family physicians, general internal medicine physicians, and pediatricians) overall was lower in rural counties than in urban counties (55.6 vs. 93.6, respectively). There were fewer general internal medicine physicians and pediatricians in rural compared to urban counties, but there was a similar number of family physicians per 100,000 population in rural and urban counties (35.0 vs. 33.9, respectively). There was substantial growth in rural nurse practitioner and physician assistant supply over the past 20 years with increases in the per capita supply more than quadrupling and tripling, respectively. Nationally, the supply of behavioral health clinicians, including psychiatrists, psychologists, psychiatric nurse practitioners, social workers, and counselors, was significantly lower in rural counties compared to urban counties. The number of behavioral health clinicians per 100,000 population in rural counties ranged from 27% (psychiatrists) to 70% (psychiatric nurse practitioners) of urban areas. The number of obstetricians per 100,000 women of childbearing age in rural counties in 2019 was less than half the number in urban counties (30.3 vs. 62.9, respectively). More than half of all U.S. rural counties lacked an obstetrician (57.4%), and more than three-quarters lacked an advanced practice midwife (75.1%) or midwife (87.4%). The supply of general surgeons per 100,000 population in rural areas in 2019 was about half of that in urban areas (6.7 vs. 13.1, respectively). The supply of general surgeons per 100,000 population decreased in both rural (-11.8%) and urban (-8.4%) areas from 1995 to 2019. 2 Policy Report • October 2024 BACKGROUND The U.S. health care system requires an adequate workforce to provide care for the population, yet rural communities often face threats to health workforce supply. These threats include challenges recruiting and retaining health professionals, an aging rural workforce, and the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic, which has led to burnout, early retirement, and deaths of rural health care workers.1–4 The scope of the challenge is vast: Over 60 percent of the primary care, mental health, and dental professional shortage areas were in rural areas as of December 2023.5 Prior research by the WWAMI Rural Health Research Center, and others, reports that the supply of many rural health care professionals, as measured in provider-to-population ratios, is lower than in urban areas. Among these professionals are general internists, pediatricians, urologists, general surgeons, nurse practitioners, registered nurses, physician assistants, pharmacists, dentists, obstetricians, midwives, psychiatrists, psychologists, psychiatric nurse practitioners, optometrists, and emergency responders.6–17 Family physicians and licensed practical nurses (LPNs) are two bright spots in that their concentration per capita is higher in rural than in urban areas. 6,15 However, rural areas have seen a greater decline over time in the density of primary care clinicians per capita than urban areas.18 Because of the lower supply of health care clinicians in rural areas, rural residents drive longer distances to obtain care and have fewer annual visits with health care clinicians than urban residents.19,20 In the past decade, the number of younger physicians entering the rural workforce has been declining, leading to aging of the rural physician workforce overall.3 In 2017, over half of rural physicians were at least 50 years old, and over a quarter were at least 60 years old.
